note: Built from the three collections of the library: every period and event of a collection that has years is here, says those years with their uncertainty, and cites the sources the collection gives for the same record. Every one of them is proposed, none is reviewed, and the comparison is not approved for the public. Left out: what has no year (Awan and Šimaški), a period that begins and ends in the same year, and a dynasty whose years are those of a period already here.
title: Iran, China and Rome side by side
summary: What ruled in Iran, in China and in Rome from the end of the third millennium BCE – Iran through the Sasanians and the caliphate to the Ghaznavids in 1030, Rome to the death of Basil II in 1025, China to the Tang in 705 – and every dated event of the three collections, side by side.

periods.label: The Median kingdom
periods.summary: The years rest on Herodotus.

periods.label: Alexander and the Seleucids in Iran
The Sasanian period
periods.summary: The rule of the Sasanian kings, from the revolt of Ardašir in 224 to the death of Yazdgard III in 651 CE.

periods.label: The Umayyad caliphate
periods.summary: The first great Muslim dynasty to rule the empire of the caliphate, from 661 to 750; Iran was governed as provinces of this Arab empire.

periods.label: The Abbasid caliphate before the Seljuks
periods.summary: From the establishment of the Abbasids in 750 until Toghril Beg’s Seljuks entered Baghdad in 1055; within it the Iranian dynasties rose in the east and the Buyids held the caliphs in tutelage.

events.label: The Assyrian sack of Susa
events.summary: Aššurbanipal destroyed Susa and the sanctuary of Dur-Untaš. The Livius pages differ on the year: 646 BCE, between 645 and 640 BCE, or the subjection of Elam in 643 BCE.

events.label: The fall of Nineveh
events.summary: The Medes under Cyaxares and the Babylonians captured the Assyrian capital Nineveh in July 612 BCE.

events.label: Cyrus defeats Astyages
events.summary: Cyrus rose against his overlord Astyages of Media; the army of Astyages revolted and handed him over, and Cyrus took Ecbatana. Livius gives 550 BCE, and mentions a chronology of 554/553.

events.label: Cyrus conquers Lydia
events.summary: Cyrus defeated Croesus of Lydia and took Sardis. The traditional year 547 BCE rests on a reading of the Nabonidus Chronicle that most scholars now doubt; it was perhaps later.

events.label: Cambyses conquers Egypt
events.summary: In 525 BCE Cambyses II conquered Egypt; the pharaoh Psammetichus III was captured alive.

events.label: Darius seizes power
events.summary: On 29 September 522 BCE Darius and six noblemen killed the king whom Darius calls the usurper Gaumâta; Darius then fought nineteen battles in one year against rebels from Persia, Elam, Media, Babylonia and other lands, the last revolt ending in December 521 BCE.

events.label: The battle of Thermopylae
events.summary: In September 480 BCE the army of Xerxes defeated the Greeks under the Spartan king Leonidas at the pass of Thermopylae.

events.label: The battle of Salamis
events.summary: At the end of September 480 BCE the Greek fleet defeated the Persian fleet at Salamis, while Xerxes watched from a hill.

events.label: The battle of Plataea
events.summary: In the summer of 479 BCE the Greeks under Pausanias defeated the Persian army of Mardonius near Plataea.

events.label: The battle of Cunaxa
events.summary: In 401 BCE Cyrus the Younger, with an army including Greek mercenaries, fought his brother Artaxerxes II at Cunaxa near Babylon; his army won, but Cyrus fell.

events.label: The reconquest of Egypt
events.summary: In 343 BCE the generals of Artaxerxes III, Bagoas and Mentor of Rhodes, reconquered Egypt.

events.label: The battle of Issus
events.summary: In November 333 BCE Alexander defeated Darius III near Issus.

events.label: The burning of Persepolis
events.summary: Alexander captured Persepolis in the first weeks of 330 BCE and burnt several palace buildings in April 330 BCE.

events.label: The death of Darius III
events.summary: In July 330 BCE Darius III, fleeing from Alexander, was murdered by his own courtiers at Choara near modern Damghan.

events.label: The weddings at Susa
events.summary: In March 324 BCE Alexander held a mass wedding at Susa where his officers married Iranian women by Persian rites; Alexander married a daughter of Darius III, and Seleucus married Apame.

events.label: The eastern campaign of Antiochus III
events.summary: Antiochus III campaigned in the east, forcing Arsaces II of Parthia (209 BCE) and the king of Bactria to accept his overlordship. Livius dates the campaign 212–205 BCE on one page and 209–204 on another.

events.label: The Parthians take Babylonia
events.summary: Mithradates I of Parthia captured Seleucia, the Seleucid capital in Babylonia, in 141 BCE – between April and June according to one Livius page, in July according to another – after taking Media; Susa followed in 139 BCE.

events.label: The defeat of Antiochus VII
events.summary: In 130 BCE Antiochus VII drove the Parthians out of Babylonia and Media; in 129 BCE they defeated him, he took his own life, and the Parthians retook all Seleucid territory in Iran.

events.label: Antony’s Parthian war
events.summary: In 36 BCE the Roman Mark Antony invaded the Parthian empire and failed; another Livius page connects his eastern campaigns with 34/33 BCE.

events.label: The return of the Roman standards
events.summary: In 20 BCE the Parthians gave back to Rome the standards they had taken from Roman armies; Augustus records it in his Res Gestae.

events.label: The settlement over Armenia
events.summary: After a Roman army surrendered to the Parthians at Rhandeia (about 62 CE), Rome and Vologases I agreed in 63 CE that his brother Tiridates would be king of Armenia.

events.label: Trajan takes Ctesiphon
events.summary: In Trajan’s war against Osroes I (114–117), the Romans took Babylon, Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 116; after Trajan’s death in 117 Hadrian gave up the conquests.

events.label: The Romans take Ctesiphon under Vologases IV
events.summary: In the war that began over Armenia in 161, the Roman general Avidius Cassius took the Parthian capital; Livius dates it to 164 on one page and 165 on another.

events.label: Septimius Severus takes Ctesiphon
events.summary: In a new war with Vologases V, the emperor Septimius Severus took Seleucia and Ctesiphon; Livius dates it to 197 on one page and 198 on another. He then failed to take Hatra.

events.label: Artabanus IV against Macrinus at Nisibis
events.summary: After Caracalla’s attack and murder, Artabanus IV met the new emperor Macrinus near Nisibis in 217; the sources present it as a Roman defeat, and Rome paid an indemnity.

events.label: Ardašir defeats Artabanus IV
events.summary: Artabanus IV marched against the insurrection of Ardašir in Persis in 224 and was defeated; a relief near Firuzabad shows the victory. It marks the beginning of the Sasanian empire.

events.label: Ardašir takes Ctesiphon
events.summary: Two years after his victory, Ardašir took Ctesiphon, the Parthian capital, and was recognised as ruler of the former Parthian empire; Ctesiphon became the city where Sasanian kings were inaugurated.

events.label: Ardašir’s war with Rome begins
events.summary: Ardašir’s siege of Nisibis began a long war with Rome; Livius dates the siege to 230 on its page on Ardašir and the first fighting on the Euphrates to 231 on its page on the Sasanians.

events.label: The defeat and death of Gordian III
events.summary: The emperor Gordian III invaded Mesopotamia in 244, was defeated near Ctesiphon and died – killed in action, or lynched by his soldiers, as the Livius pages differ; his successor Philip made a peace that left Armenia to the Persians.

events.label: Shapur captures Valerian
events.summary: In 260 Shapur I defeated the Roman emperor Valerian and took him captive; reliefs at Bishapur and Naqš-e Rustam show the triumph, and the captured soldiers built Bishapur.

events.label: Carus takes Ctesiphon
events.summary: The emperor Carus took Ctesiphon in 283; Bahram II lost the war and with it Armenia and northern Mesopotamia.

events.label: The peace of 298
events.summary: After Galerius defeated Narseh, a treaty concluded at Nisibis in 298 made the Persians give up territories in northern Mesopotamia and gave Rome lands east of the Tigris.

events.label: Shapur II takes Amida
events.summary: The Sasanian king Shapur II captured the Roman city of Amida in 359.

events.label: The death of Julian and the peace of 363
events.summary: The emperor Julian invaded Mesopotamia and reached Ctesiphon, but was defeated by Shapur II and killed in action on 26 June 363; his successor Jovian made a peace that gave up Nisibis and other eastern lands.

events.label: Armenia divided
events.summary: In 387 Shapur III made peace with Rome, and Armenia was divided between the two empires.

events.label: Bahram V takes the throne with Lakhmid help
events.summary: Bahram V, brought up at the Lakhmid court of Hira, gained the throne at Ctesiphon in 420 with the help of the Lakhmid king against the nobles who had killed his brother Shapur.

events.label: Bahram V’s war with Rome
events.summary: A brief war between Bahram V and the Romans in 421–422.

events.label: Yazdgard II invades Roman Armenia
events.summary: In 451 Yazdgard II invaded the Roman province of Armenia; the borders in the end remained unchanged.

events.label: Peroz I killed in battle
events.summary: Peroz I was killed in action in 484 – Livius places the war in the northeast on one page and on the northwestern frontier on another – which brought a crisis on the Sasanian empire.

events.label: Peroz’s campaigns against the Hephthalites
events.summary: Peroz I led three disastrous campaigns against the Hephthalites: in the first he was forced to surrender, in the third, in 484, he died with his cavalry in a hidden ditch. The Shahnameh gives the fullest account of his defeats.

events.label: Kavad I takes Amida
events.summary: Kavad I attacked the Byzantine empire and captured Amida in 502/503; a second Roman attempt in the winter of 505 recovered it, but the Romans had to pay the Persian garrison to leave.

events.label: The Mazdakites suppressed
events.summary: Khusrau I suppressed the religious movement called Mazdakism in the 530s; its adherents may have fled to Arabia.

events.label: Khusrau I takes Antioch
events.summary: In 540 Khusrau I conquered Antioch, the capital of Roman Syria, and settled its people in a new city near Ctesiphon, "Khusrau’s Antioch".

events.label: The Hephthalites crushed near Bukhara
events.summary: Between 558 and 561 Khusrau I, acting with the newly arrived Turks, crushed the Hephthalites in a great battle near Bukhara, and the two powers divided their land along the Oxus.

events.label: The revolt of Bahram VI
events.summary: In 590 the general Bahram VI revolted and marched west; Hormizd IV was executed and his son Khusrau II fled to the Byzantines, who brought him back in 591.

events.label: The end of the Lakhmids
events.summary: Khusrau II had the Lakhmid king Noʿmān III killed in 602 and soon after brought Hira under direct Persian rule, removing the Arab bulwark of Iraq.

events.label: The battle of Ḏu Qār
events.summary: In 604 the Banu Bakr defeated a Persian force at Ḏu Qār, which Tabari saw as a consequence of Khusrau II’s action against Noʿmān.

events.label: The Persians take Jerusalem
events.summary: The armies of Khusrau II under Shahrbaraz took Antioch in 612 and Damascus in 613, and sacked Jerusalem in 614, carrying off the relic of the True Cross.

events.label: The Persians take Alexandria
events.summary: The armies of Khusrau II invaded Egypt and captured Alexandria in 619, cutting the corn supply of Constantinople.

events.label: The Persians before Constantinople
events.summary: In 626 Persian forces under Shahrbaraz reached the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, a mile from Constantinople, while the Avars besieged the city; they could not take it.

events.label: Heraclius defeats the Persians near Nineveh
events.summary: In December 627 Heraclius, who had invaded Mesopotamia, defeated a large Persian army near the ruins of Nineveh.

events.label: The fall of Khusrau II
events.summary: After the defeat, the army mutinied; early in 628 the crown prince Sheroe imprisoned his father Khusrau II, who died soon after, and became king as Kavad II.

events.label: The True Cross returned to Jerusalem
events.summary: After peace was made, Heraclius returned the relic of the True Cross to Jerusalem in 630.

events.label: The first Arab invasion of Mesopotamia
events.summary: In 633 an army of Christians and Muslims invaded Mesopotamia; a Sasanian counteroffensive was followed by an Arab one.

events.label: The Arabs take Ctesiphon
events.summary: The Arabs captured Ctesiphon, the beginning of their conquest of Mesopotamia; Livius dates it to 636 on its page on the Sasanians and to 637 on its page on Ctesiphon.

events.label: The battle of Nehavand
events.summary: The Arabs invaded Iran and defeated Yazdgard III at Nehavand, after which he retreated to the northeast; Livius dates it to 641 on one page and 642 on another.

events.label: The Arabs take Istakhr
events.summary: The walled city of Istakhr repulsed a first Arab attack in about 644, but was captured and sacked in about 650.

events.label: The death of Yazdgard III
events.summary: Yazdgard III, the last Sasanian king, died as a fugitive in 651, ten years after Nehavand; with him the Sasanian empire ended.

events.label: The Abbasid revolution
events.summary: On 15 June 747 Abu Muslim raised the banner of revolt in Khorasan; it triumphed in 750 when the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II was defeated and killed, and the Abbasids took the caliphate.

events.label: The death of Abu Muslim
events.summary: Suspicious of a vassal with so much power, the caliph al-Mansur took Khorasan from Abu Muslim and had him put to death at court in February 755; his unavenged death inspired many later revolts.

events.label: The founding of Baghdad
events.summary: In 762 Baghdad was founded on the Tigris as the capital of the Abbasid caliphs.

events.label: al-Maʾmun defeats his brother Amin
events.summary: From his governorate in Marv, with the men and resources of Persia, al-Maʾmun defeated his brother Amin in 813, whose cause was that of the Arabs of Iraq and Syria.

events.label: Yaʿqub hailed as amir in Sistan
events.summary: Out of the power struggles of the ʿayyar leaders of Sistan, Yaʿqub emerged the victor and was hailed as amir by the army of Sistan in 861.

events.label: Yaʿqub at Nishapur
events.summary: In 873 Yaʿqub intervened at Nishapur and ended the rule of the Tahirid governors in Khorasan.

events.label: The battle of Dayr al-ʿAqul
events.summary: Marching on Baghdad, Yaʿqub was decisively defeated by the regent al-Muwaffaq at Dayr al-ʿAqul southeast of Baghdad in 876; he kept Fars and Ahvaz.

events.label: ʿAmr b. Layth defeated outside Balkh
events.summary: In 900 Ismaʿil the Samanid crossed the Oxus and defeated ʿAmr b. Layth outside Balkh, capturing him and overturning Saffarid power in a single day; Khorasan passed to the Samanids for almost a century.

events.label: The murder of Mardavij
events.summary: In 935 Mardavij was killed by his Turkish slaves; his empire fell apart and most of its lands south of the Caspian mountains went to the Buyid brothers.

events.label: The Buyids enter Baghdad
events.summary: On 19 December 945 Ahmad b. Buya entered Baghdad without a fight and the Buyids took the caliphs into their tutelage.

events.label: ʿAdud al-Dawla as shahanshah
events.summary: A coin struck in Fars in 970 shows ʿAdud al-Dawla as a crowned king with the inscription shahanshah.

events.label: Ferdowsi begins the Shahnameh
events.summary: About 977, after the death of Daqiqi, Ferdowsi began writing the Shahnameh; a first version was complete by 994.

events.label: Mahmud throws off Samanid authority
events.summary: In 999 Mahmud of Ghazni threw off Samanid authority; with the Qarakhanids north of the Oxus he divided up the former Samanid lands, and the Samanid dynasty came to its end.

events.label: The completion of the Shahnameh
events.summary: In his seventy-first year, on 8 March 1010, Ferdowsi finished the Shahnameh.

events.label: Mahmud takes Ray
events.summary: In 1029 Mahmud of Ghazni conquered Ray, until then the capital of the northern Buyid emirate.

events.label: Biruni completes his India
events.summary: In 1030, just after the death of Mahmud, Biruni completed his great work on India, the Tahqiq ma li’l-Hind.

periods.label: The Xia (tradition)
periods.summary: The first dynasty in Chinese tradition, said to have been founded by Yu the Great; there is no written evidence of it, though many historians identify Erlitou as its capital. The traditional dates differ: about 2100 or 1900 to 1600 BCE.

periods.label: The Spring and Autumn period
periods.summary: The first part of the Eastern Zhou, from 770 BCE to about 480–475 BCE.

periods.label: The Warring States
periods.summary: From about 480–475 BCE to the unification under the Qin in 221 BCE, when the many small states were consolidated into seven kingdoms.

periods.label: The Three Kingdoms
periods.summary: Wei, Shu-Han and Wu, which divided China after the fall of the Han; Britannica dates the period 220–280, to the fall of Wu, and Asia for Educators 220–265.

periods.label: The Western Jin
periods.summary: A short time of relative order after the Three Kingdoms, which ended with the fall of Luoyang in 311 and Chang’an in 316.

periods.label: The Sixteen Kingdoms
periods.summary: The short-lived non-Chinese states that ruled northern China from 303 until the Northern Wei unified it in 439.

periods.label: The Eastern Jin
periods.summary: The Jin court set up at Jiankang in 317 by a member of the imperial family, ruled by the great southern families until 420.

periods.label: The Northern Wei
periods.summary: The Tuoba state in the north; Britannica dates it 386–534/535 and Asia for Educators 386–535, and the Smithsonian says it brought all of north China under its rule in 439.

periods.label: The Southern Dynasties
periods.summary: The Liu-Song, Southern Qi, Southern Liang and Southern Chen, which ruled the south from Jiankang from 420 until the Sui overthrew the last of them in 589.

periods.label: The Sui
periods.summary: The reunification of China under the Sui, from 581 to 618.

periods.label: The Tang
periods.summary: The rule of the Tang, from 618 to 907; this collection follows it to 705.

events.label: The Zhou conquest of the Shang
events.summary: The Zhou under King Wu overthrew the Shang. The sources give about 1050 or 1046 BCE.

events.label: The fall of the Western Zhou
events.summary: In 771 BCE the Western Zhou fell; the court moved east to Luoyang.

events.label: The fall of the Qin
events.summary: The Qin fell in 206 BCE; Xiang Yu burnt Xianyang in 207 BCE.

events.label: Zhang Qian travels to the west
The restoration of the Han
events.summary: In the autumn of 25 CE Liu Xiu claimed the imperial title and restored the Han; Wang Mang had died in 23 CE.

events.label: The expedition against the Xiongnu
events.summary: In 73 CE Emperor Ming sent an army against the Xiongnu; in the same winter Ban Chao arrested Dou Ti.

events.label: Gan Ying’s journey toward Da Qin
The great Qiang rebellion
events.summary: A mutiny of auxiliaries in the northwest grew in 107 into a full-scale rebellion of the Qiang within China, which lasted until 118.

events.label: Envoys from Rome at the Han court
events.summary: In 166 men who called themselves ambassadors from the Roman empire came to the court of Emperor Huan.

events.label: The Yellow Turban rebellion
events.summary: In the spring of 184 the Yellow Turbans, a popular sect led by Zhang Jue, rose and ravaged the north and east; the warlordism that followed ended the Han.

events.label: Dong Zhuo takes power
events.summary: In 189 eunuchs and the general He Jin destroyed each other at Luoyang; the general Dong Zhuo took power, deposed Liu Bian and in 190 moved the capital to Chang’an.

events.label: The battle of Guandu
events.summary: In 200 Yuan Shao attacked Cao Cao and was defeated at Guandu.

events.label: The battle of the Red Cliffs
events.summary: In 208 Cao Cao, who had taken over north China, was defeated at the Red Cliffs on the Yangtze by the forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei.

events.label: The end of the Han
events.summary: In the winter of 220 Emperor Xian abdicated to Cao Pi, who proclaimed himself emperor of the Wei dynasty.

events.label: Wei conquers Shu-Han
events.summary: Wei conquered the Shu-Han kingdom in 263/264.

events.label: The Jin legal code
events.summary: The court of Wudi of Jin established one of China’s earliest legal codes in 268.

events.label: The Jin reunite China
events.summary: In 280 the Jin armies of Sima Yan overran Wu, the last of the Three Kingdoms, and China was nominally reunited.

events.label: The fall of Luoyang
events.summary: In 311 the Xiongnu armies that Liu Yuan had led into northern China took and destroyed Luoyang.

events.label: The fall of Chang’an
events.summary: The fall of Chang’an in 316 ended Chinese dynastic rule in the north for centuries.

events.label: The last Western Jin emperor surrenders
events.summary: In 316 the Jin emperor, a grandson of Wudi, surrendered to a chief of the Xiongnu, abdicated and was later put to death.

events.label: A Jin court at Jiankang
events.summary: In 317 a member of the Jin imperial family set up a refugee court at Jiankang, the start of the Eastern Jin.

events.label: The Eastern Jin reconquer Sichuan
events.summary: In 347 the general Huan Wen reconquered Sichuan for the Eastern Jin; he later deposed the reigning emperor.

events.label: The gathering at the Orchid Pavilion
events.summary: Some 42 literary figures met at the Orchid Pavilion during the Spring Purification Festival of 353 to compose poems; Wang Xizhi wrote the preface to their poems.

events.label: The battle of the Fei River
events.summary: In 383 the Eastern Jin turned back the invading armies of the northern nomads at the Fei River.

events.label: The uprising of the landowners
events.summary: An uprising led by disaffected landowners began in 400 and was crushed in 402, giving army leaders more power.

events.label: The Eastern Jin push northwest
events.summary: Between 415 and 417 the Eastern Jin pushed northwestward and regained access to the trade routes of Central Asia.

events.label: The Northern Wei unify the north
events.summary: In 439 the Northern Wei brought the whole of north China under its rule, ending the Sixteen Kingdoms.

events.label: The equal-field system
events.summary: In 485 Xiaowendi of the Northern Wei introduced the equal-field system, which assigned land to every peasant family.

events.label: The Northern Zhou reunify the north
events.summary: After the Wei broke apart soon after 520, the Northern Zhou reunified northern China in 577.

events.label: The Sui reunite China
events.summary: In 589 Yang Jian crossed the Yangtze and overthrew the last southern dynasty at Jiankang, uniting China under one government after almost four centuries.

events.label: The Grand Canal begun
events.summary: In 608 Yangdi built a great canal between the rice-growing south and the Beijing area, and in 610 extended it, beginning the Grand Canal network.

events.label: The Sui expeditions against Korea
events.summary: Yangdi’s three expeditions against the Koreans between 612 and 614 ended in disaster and led to revolts.

events.label: The Tang proclaimed
events.summary: Li Yuan rose in rebellion in 617, took Chang’an and in 618 proclaimed the Tang dynasty.

events.label: The Xuanwu gate incident
events.summary: In 626 Li Shimin ambushed and killed his two brothers at the Xuanwu gate of the palace; two months later his father abdicated in his favour.

events.label: Xuanzang’s journey to India
events.summary: The monk Xuanzang left for India in 629 and came back to China in 645 with the scriptures he had gathered.

events.label: Korea made a vassal
events.summary: Continuing his father’s campaigns, Gaozong conquered the Korean peninsula and made Korea a vassal state in 668.

events.label: Wuhou takes the throne
events.summary: After ruling through puppets since Gaozong’s death in 683, Wu Zhao usurped the throne herself in 690.

events.label: Wuhou forced to abdicate
events.summary: In 705 Wuhou’s ministers and generals seized the palace and forced her to abdicate in favour of her son Zhongzong.

periods.label: The Roman monarchy
periods.summary: The kings and their years rest on tradition.

periods.label: The year of the four emperors
periods.summary: The civil war after Nero’s death, when Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian were emperors in turn.

periods.label: The Antonines
periods.summary: The family of Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Lucius Verus and Commodus, who ruled from about 138 to 192; their years are often called the golden age of the empire.

periods.label: The Severans
periods.summary: The dynasty of Septimius Severus, which ruled from 193 to 235 with a break in 217–218.

periods.label: The first tetrarchy
periods.summary: The rule of two augusti, Diocletian and Maximian, with two caesares, Galerius and Constantius, from 293 until the augusti resigned in 305.

periods.label: The Constantinian dynasty
periods.summary: The family of Constantine the Great, which ruled the empire or parts of it from 305 to 363; under it Christianity was no longer persecuted and Constantinople was founded.

periods.label: The Valentinian dynasty
periods.summary: The family of Valentinian I, which ruled the empire or parts of it from 363 to 392, in a western and an eastern branch.

periods.label: The Theodosian dynasty
periods.summary: The dynasty of Theodosius I, which ruled from 378 to 457; his sons founded an eastern and a western line, and in its time Britain and Gaul were lost and Constantinople became the chief city of the empire.

periods.label: The divided empire, west
periods.summary: The western half of the empire under its own emperors, from the death of Theodosius I in 395 to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476.

periods.label: The Heraclian dynasty
periods.summary: The house of Heraclius, which ruled from 610 to 711; under his successors Egypt, Syria and Africa were lost to the Arabs, Constantinople withstood a four-year siege and the Bulgars settled south of the Danube.

periods.label: The Isaurian dynasty
periods.summary: The house of Leo III, which ruled from 717 to 802; it turned back the Arabs from Constantinople and began the attack on the veneration of icons, and ended with the deposition of Irene.

periods.label: The age of Iconoclasm
periods.summary: From the accession of Leo III in 717 to 867 the emperors tried, often with wide support, to end the veneration of icons; Irene restored it at the Council of Nicaea in 787, Leo V renewed iconoclasm in 815, and the icons were finally restored in 843.

periods.label: The Amorian dynasty
periods.summary: The house of Michael II, also called Phrygian, which ruled from 820 to 867 through his son Theophilus and grandson Michael III; under it the icons were finally restored in 843.

periods.label: The Macedonian dynasty
periods.summary: The house of Basil I, who murdered his way to the throne in 867; until the death of Basil II in 1025 the empire enjoyed a golden age, recovering Crete, Antioch and Bulgaria.

events.label: The founding of Rome
events.summary: According to tradition Romulus founded Rome on the Palatine on 21 April 753 BCE; Livius calls this Varronian date an artificial calculation.

events.label: The Twelve Tables
events.summary: The first codification of Roman law, written by a board of ten men in the middle of the fifth century BCE: ten tables in 451 and two more in 450 BCE in the traditional chronology.

events.label: The Gauls take Rome
events.summary: After their victory at the Allia the Gauls occupied Rome and besieged the Capitol until the Romans bought their freedom with gold – in 390 BCE in the traditional chronology, in 387 or 386 according to Livius.

events.label: The Licinian-Sextian laws
events.summary: Laws first proposed in 376 and passed in 367 BCE (traditional chronology) that opened the consulship to plebeians, adjusted debts and limited the ownership of public land.

events.label: The First Punic War
events.summary: The war of Rome and Carthage from 264 to 241 BCE, in which Rome conquered Sicily.

events.label: The Second Punic War
events.summary: The war of Rome and Carthage from 218 to 202 BCE, in which Hannibal crossed the Alps; the peace was signed in 201 BCE.

events.label: The battle of Cannae
events.summary: On 2 August 216 BCE Hannibal destroyed the army of the two Roman consuls at Cannae.

events.label: The battle of Zama
events.summary: On 19 October 202 BCE Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama in Africa.

events.label: The Third Punic War
events.summary: The last war against Carthage, begun in 149 BCE after Cato had urged it; it ended in 146 BCE with the destruction of the city.

events.label: The destruction of Carthage
events.summary: In 146 BCE Rome took and sacked Carthage; Corinth was sacked in the same year.

events.label: The tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus
events.summary: In 133 BCE Tiberius Gracchus proposed his land bill; he was killed on the Capitol in the same year.

events.label: The Social War
events.summary: The war with Rome’s Italian allies, which began in 91 BCE; citizenship was promised to loyal allies in 90 and to those who surrendered in 89. Marius and Sulla fought on the Roman side.

events.label: The revolt of Spartacus
events.summary: A slave revolt that began at Capua and was suppressed by Crassus; the Livius page dates the war 73–71 BCE in one place and 73–70 in another.

events.label: The alliance of Caesar, Crassus and Pompey
events.summary: In 60 BCE Caesar, Crassus and Pompey made a private agreement, sealed by Pompey’s marriage to Caesar’s daughter Julia; modern historians call it the First Triumvirate.

events.label: Caesar conquers Gaul
events.summary: From 58 to 50 BCE Caesar conquered Gaul; in 52 BCE Vercingetorix surrendered to him at Alesia.

events.label: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
events.summary: In the night of 10/11 January 49 BCE Caesar crossed the Rubicon, the border of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy, and began the second civil war; where the river was is not certain.

events.label: The battle of Pharsalus
events.summary: On 9 August 48 BCE Caesar defeated Pompey at Pharsalus; Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered there.

events.label: The murder of Caesar
events.summary: On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, Caesar was murdered by a group led by Gaius Cassius, Decimus Brutus and Marcus Junius Brutus.

events.label: The Second Triumvirate
events.summary: In 43 BCE Antony and Octavian became triumvirs with a third colleague, an official magistracy with dictatorial powers.

events.label: The battle of Philippi
events.summary: In October 42 BCE Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi.

events.label: The settlement of Augustus
events.summary: In January 27 BCE Octavian accepted the title Augustus (16 January); the rule of the emperors begins here.

events.label: The battle in the Teutoburg Forest
events.summary: In September 9 CE Arminius, leading a coalition of Germanic tribes, annihilated three Roman legions under Publius Quintilius Varus; Germania remained independent.

events.label: The death of Augustus
events.summary: Augustus died on 19 August 14 CE and Tiberius succeeded him.

events.label: The Great Fire of Rome
events.summary: The great fire of Rome in 64 CE, under Nero.

events.label: The Jewish War
events.summary: The war in Judaea that began in 66 CE and culminated in the destruction of the temple of Jerusalem in 70; the last resistance at Masada held out until 74.

events.label: The death of Nero
events.summary: After the revolts of Vindex, Macer and Galba Nero took his own life in June 68 CE – on 9 June according to his page, on 8 June according to the chronology of 68–70.

events.label: The siege of Jerusalem
events.summary: Titus began the siege of Jerusalem on 14 April 70 CE and was master of the city on 8 September.

events.label: The eruption of Vesuvius
events.summary: In 79 CE, in the reign of Titus, Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii.

events.label: The dedication of the Colosseum
events.summary: The Amphitheatrum Flavium, built by Vespasian, was dedicated by Titus in 80 CE.

events.label: The murder of Domitian
events.summary: Domitian was murdered by courtiers on 18 September 96 CE; Nerva became emperor the same day.

events.label: Trajan becomes emperor
events.summary: On Nerva’s death in January 98 CE Trajan, his adopted son, became emperor.

events.label: The revolt of Bar Kochba
events.summary: A Jewish insurrection that began in 132 under Hadrian; Hadrian took Bethar in 135/136 and the last fighting in Galilee was in 136.

events.label: The plague under Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: A plague broke out in 165, during the Parthian war, and reached Rome in 167.

events.label: The year of the five emperors
events.summary: After the murder of Pertinax in 193, Didius Julianus, Pescennius Niger, Clodius Albinus and Septimius Severus were all proclaimed emperor; Severus won the civil wars that followed.

events.label: Citizenship for all free men
events.summary: In 212 Caracalla gave Roman citizenship to all free-born men of the empire.

events.label: Shapur captures Valerian
events.summary: In 260 the emperor Valerian was defeated and taken captive by the Sasanian king Shapur I; he died in captivity in 262, and in the following years many usurpers rose in the empire.

events.label: A new wall for Rome
events.summary: In 271 Aurelian ordered the building of a new wall around Rome.

events.label: Aurelian takes Palmyra
events.summary: In 272 Aurelian defeated Zenobia and her son Vaballathus and captured Palmyra; in 274 he defeated the Gallic emperor Tetricus.

events.label: The first tetrarchy
events.summary: In 293 Diocletian and Maximian each appointed a caesar, Galerius and Constantius, who were to succeed them.

events.label: Diocletian and Maximian resign
events.summary: In May 305 the two augusti laid down their power, and the caesares Galerius and Constantius became augusti – for the first time in ages a transfer of power without bloodshed.

events.label: The battle of the Milvian Bridge
events.summary: In 312 Constantine crossed the Alps and defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge, where Maxentius was killed.

events.label: The meeting at Milan
events.summary: In 313 Constantine and Licinius met at Milan; the agreement is known as the Edict of Milan.

events.label: The founding of Constantinople
events.summary: After defeating Licinius in 324, Constantine became sole ruler and founded a new residence at Byzantium, Constantinople.

events.label: The Council of Nicaea
events.summary: The first ecumenical council of the Church met at Nicaea from 20 May to 19 June 325.

events.label: The death of Julian and the peace of 363
events.summary: Julian invaded the Sasanian empire and was killed in action on 26 June 363; Jovian then made a peace with Shapur II that gave up Nisibis.

events.label: The battle of Adrianople
events.summary: In 378 the Goths defeated and killed the emperor Valens at Adrianople, and Theodosius was made emperor in the east.

events.label: The empire divided between two sons
events.summary: At the death of Theodosius I in 395, his sons Arcadius and Honorius succeeded him in the east and the west.

events.label: The Visigoths take Rome
events.summary: In 410 the Visigoths captured Rome; Alaric died the same year, and Britain was evacuated.

events.label: The Vandals take Carthage
events.summary: The Vandals invaded Africa in 429 and took Carthage in 439.

events.label: Attila defeated in Gaul
events.summary: In 451 the Huns crossed the Rhine and invaded Gaul; Aetius defeated Attila near Troyes. In 452 the Huns invaded Italy.

events.label: The Vandals sack Rome
events.summary: In 455, after the murder of Valentinian III and the death of Petronius Maximus, the Vandals sacked Rome.

events.label: The end of the empire in the west
events.summary: In 476 the soldiers in Italy revolted and their leader Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor in the west.

events.label: Theodoric conquers Italy
events.summary: The Ostrogoths under Theodoric invaded Italy in 488 and by 493 had conquered almost the whole peninsula and Sicily, ending the rule of Odoacer.

events.label: Belisarius defeats the Persians
events.summary: Belisarius won his first victory as a commander against Sasanian Persia on the Mesopotamian front in 530.

events.label: The Nika riots
events.summary: In January 532 the Nika riots broke out in Constantinople under Justinian.

events.label: Roman law codified
events.summary: In 533 the codification of Roman law, the Institutes and the Digest, was completed under Justinian.

events.label: Belisarius conquers Africa
events.summary: Justinian’s general Belisarius conquered Africa and entered Carthage on 15 September 534; he went on to Sicily and took Rome in 536.

events.label: The Hagia Sophia inaugurated
events.summary: The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople was inaugurated on 26 December 537.

events.label: Narses conquers Italy
events.summary: Justinian’s general Narses completed the conquest of Italy in 552.

events.label: The Langobards invade Italy
events.summary: In 568, under Justin II, the Langobards invaded Italy.

events.label: Heraclius defeats the Persians near Nineveh
events.summary: In December 627 Heraclius defeated a large Persian army near the ruins of Nineveh; Khusrau II fell soon after, and in 630 Heraclius returned the True Cross to Jerusalem.

events.label: Alexandria capitulates to the Arabs
events.summary: Alexandria capitulated in 642, removing Egypt forever from Byzantine authority.

events.label: The Arab siege of Constantinople
events.summary: After their assaults on Armenia and Asia Minor the Arabs besieged Constantinople for four years, from 674 to 678; Constantine IV withstood them, a turning point in European history.

events.label: The sixth ecumenical council
events.summary: The sixth general council, summoned by Constantine IV in 680–681 at Constantinople, condemned Monothelitism.

events.label: The Bulgar kingdom recognised
events.summary: Constantine IV failed to defeat the Bulgars in 681 and by treaty recognised them as an independent kingdom south of the Danube.

events.label: Justinian II deposed
events.summary: Justinian II was deposed and mutilated in 695; with Bulgar help he returned to the throne in 705.

events.label: The loss of Africa
events.summary: By the end of the seventh century Africa was largely lost to the Muslims, who in 711 seized the last outpost at Septem.

events.label: The second Arab siege of Constantinople
events.summary: In 717 the Arabs again besieged Constantinople by land and sea; with Bulgar help Leo III turned back the assault in 718.

events.label: The battle of Akroinon
events.summary: With the help of the Khazars, Leo III’s reign ended with a major victory over the Arabs at Akroinon in 740.

events.label: The Council of Nicaea restores the icons
events.summary: At the instigation of the empress Irene, the Council of Nicaea in 787 restored the veneration of icons.

events.label: Irene rules alone
events.summary: Irene had her son Constantine VI deposed and blinded and ruled alone from 797 until a revolt of palace officials deposed her in 802.

events.label: The coronation of Charlemagne
events.summary: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks and Lombards, emperor of the Romans, a challenge to the emperor at Constantinople.

events.label: Nikephoros I falls against Krum
events.summary: Nikephoros I led his army against the Bulgar khan Krum in 811 and met defeat and death.

events.label: Leo V renews iconoclasm
events.summary: After military reverses, Leo V revived the iconoclast policies of Constantine V in 815.

events.label: The Arabs take Crete
events.summary: In 826 or 827 the Arabs captured Crete, a sign of the decline of Byzantine strength in the Mediterranean.

events.label: Theophilus defeated and Amorium lost
events.summary: In 838 a Muslim army defeated Theophilus himself and went on to capture the fortress of Amorium in Asia Minor.

events.label: The icons restored
events.summary: In 843, under Michael III, the icons were definitively restored and their veneration proclaimed as Orthodox belief.

events.label: The Rus attack Constantinople
events.summary: Sailing down the Dnieper from Kiev to the Black Sea, the warships of the Rus first attacked Constantinople in 860.

events.label: Basil I seizes the throne
events.summary: In 867 Basil I murdered his way to the throne and founded the Macedonian dynasty.

events.label: The Arabs complete the conquest of Sicily
events.summary: In 902 the Arabs completed the conquest of Sicily, though they were kept out of Byzantine South Italy.

events.label: Simeon of Bulgaria before Constantinople
events.summary: In 913 Simeon I of Bulgaria brought his army to the walls of Constantinople, demanding the imperial title.

events.label: Crete reconquered
events.summary: In 961 Nikephoros Phokas reconquered Crete and destroyed the Arab fleet that had terrorised the Aegean for 150 years.

events.label: Antioch recaptured
events.summary: In 969 the Byzantine armies recaptured Antioch, seat of one of the patriarchs.

events.label: John Tzimiskes humbles the Rus and Bulgaria
events.summary: In 971 John Tzimiskes humiliated the Rus and reduced Bulgaria to a client kingdom.

events.label: The baptism of Vladimir of Kiev
events.summary: Vladimir of Kiev, who had helped Basil II to keep his throne, received the emperor’s sister in marriage and was baptised in 989.

events.label: Bulgaria subdued
events.summary: After a ruthless campaign of some twenty years Basil II crushed the last Bulgarian resistance by 1018.

events.label: The death of Basil II
events.summary: Basil II died in 1025 while preparing a campaign against the Arabs in Sicily; with him ended the golden age of the Macedonian era.
